title: World Energy Investment 2026, Executive summary
date_evidence: The IEA's 2026 World Energy Investment report was released in Paris on 28 May 2026. Global energy investment is expected to reach 3.4 trillion dollars in 2026, a 5 per cent rise from 2025.
key_claim: Global energy investment reaches roughly USD 3.4 trillion in 2026, with about USD 2.2 trillion to clean supply; grid investment approaches USD 550 billion (up nearly 20% YoY) and battery storage tops USD 100 billion, yet over 2,500 GW of projects sit stalled in grid queues.
frame_summary: Argues that energy investment is rising but increasingly mismatched: capital flows to generation and clean technology while grids and storage lag, making delivery infrastructure the binding constraint on the transition.
verbatim_quote: Global energy investment is expected to reach 3.4 trillion dollars in 2026, a 5 per cent rise from 2025. About 2.2 trillion dollars will go to grids, storage, low-emissions fuels, nuclear, renewables, energy efficiency and electrification, while the remaining 1.2 trillion dollars will be invested in oil, gas and coal. Grid investment is set to approach 550 billion dollars, up nearly 20 per cent year on year, while battery storage investment is expected to exceed 100 billion dollars. Over 2,500 GW of renewable, large-load and storage projects are currently stalled in grid queues worldwide.
cluster: Delivery, not generation, now sets the pace

title: Extreme weather and uneven climate adaptation challenge Europe's resilience
key_claim: Europe has logged EUR 822 billion in weather and climate losses over 1980-2024, a quarter of them in 2021-2024; all member countries now have adaptation policies but implementation lags, and the European Commission's Integrated Framework for Climate Resilience is due by end-2026.
frame_summary: Argues that Europe's climate impacts are intensifying faster than adaptation is being implemented, so resilience must move from planning to financed, enforced action.
verbatim_quote: The European Union has registered EUR 822 billion total losses in the period of 1980-2024, with 25% of these losses registered between 2021 and 2024. The report comes ahead of the European Commission's expected publication of a European Integrated Framework for Climate Resilience, due by the end of 2026. Only 16% of small municipalities have adaptation action plans, compared to 28% of larger ones.

title: Notice 2025-42: Beginning of Construction for Sections 45Y and 48E
date_evidence: IRS Notice 2025-42, released August 15, 2025, provides guidance on how taxpayers can establish the beginning of construction of a wind or solar facility for purposes of the credit termination provisions added to Sections 45Y and 48E.
key_claim: Treasury's Notice 2025-42 makes the Physical Work Test the exclusive way for most wind and solar projects to establish that construction began before the OBBBA 4 July 2026 cliff, eliminating the 5% safe harbour for projects above 1.5 MW.
frame_summary: Implements and argues that wind and solar must meet a stricter physical-work construction-start test to qualify before the OBBBA cliff, deliberately tightening the clean-energy tax-credit window.
signals_supported: US clean-energy tax-credit cliff and offshore-wind retreat
verbatim_quote: Wind and solar facilities must either be placed in service by December 31, 2027, or begin construction within one year after enactment of the OBBB (by July 4, 2026). The Physical Work Test is the exclusive method for establishing that construction has begun on an applicable wind or solar facility before July 5, 2026.

title: Global Electricity Review 2026
date_evidence: Ember releases seventh annual Global Electricity Review 2026 (Vision IAS current-affairs, 2026-04-22); the report covers global electricity generation in 2025 and was released in April 2026.
key_claim: For the first time in a century, renewables (33.8% of generation) overtook coal (33.0%) in the global electricity mix in 2025; solar alone met about 75% of demand growth and wind and solar together met 99%.
frame_summary: Argues that clean generation has now structurally overtaken coal in the global mix and is meeting essentially all demand growth, marking an inflection in the power transition.
signals_supported: Renewables overtake coal in the mix
verbatim_quote: For the first time in 100 years, renewables (33.8%, 10,730 TWh) overtook coal power (33.0%, 10,476 TWh) in the global electricity mix. Solar alone met 75% of the increase in global electricity demand, while together with wind it accounted for 99% of demand growth.
